n0001.title: Forms of Memory in Post-colonial Australia
n0001.gist: The essay argues that post-colonial Australia's varied practices of remembering—through Indigenous poetry and the Federal Apology—must remain hauntedly open to the past while still enabling hopeful movement into the future.

n0012.navLabel: The brown-skin lycanthrope's beliefs are swallowed and regurgitated in foreign lands for a dollar

n0016.title: Hauntings
n0016.gist: Drawing on Huggan, Derrida and Freud, the essay distinguishes haunting from mourning and melancholy to ask whether post-colonial remembering can be hopeful rather than merely wounded.

n0017.title: Gothic Wound Culture
n0017.gist: Huggan's notion of a 'gothic' critical period obsessed with trauma sets up the essay's central tension between wound-focused mourning and productive haunting.

n0019.navLabel: Huggan's 'gothic period' of wound culture sets up the tension between mourning and haunted remembering

n0020.title: Derrida and Freud on Ghosts
n0020.gist: Derrida's uninvited ghosts and Freud's account of inconsolable mourning complicate Huggan's claim that mourning simply domesticates the past.

n0021.navLabel: Derrida's untimely ghosts, drawn on by Huggan, are anti-commemorative unlike domesticating mourning

n0022.navLabel: Ghosts move freely between past and present, confronting us against our will despite mourning's reparative work

n0023.navLabel: The essay questions Huggan's 'despite' and 'mourning' against Freud's mourning/melancholy distinction

n0024.navLabel: Freud's letter says we remain inconsolable, never finding a substitute, and this is how it should be

n0025.title: Mourning versus Melancholy
n0025.gist: Revisiting Freud's mourning/melancholy distinction, the essay asks whether post-colonial nationhood can move toward hopeful remembering rather than perpetual melancholic loss.

n0026.navLabel: Freud's mourning empties the world while melancholia empties the ego, raising hope for post-colonial remembering

n0027.navLabel: The essay asks whether memory can take the form of hope, informed by the past yet threading toward an unknown future

n0028.title: The Apology and the Future
n0028.gist: Analysing the 2008 Apology to the Stolen Generations, the essay critiques its rhetoric of moving into the future and asks how genuine hauntedness might still inform reconciliation.

n0029.title: Apology's Rhetoric and Pronouns
n0029.gist: The Apology's language and collective pronouns are shown to distance the speaking 'we' from the Indigenous 'other' even as it invokes reflection.

n0031.navLabel: The Apology's 360 words repeat 'future' 13 times, prompting questions about remembering

n0032.navLabel: The Apology's opening honours Indigenous peoples and calls for moving forward with confidence to the future

n0033.navLabel: The collective 'we' in the Apology's rhetoric excludes the Indigenous other even while asking reflection

n0034.title: Turning to the Future
n0034.gist: The Apology's repeated turn toward 'the future' risks foreclosing genuine mourning and glossing over unresolved injustice.

n0035.navLabel: Little space for mournful reflection remains as the Apology's temporal framework moves quickly to the future

n0036.navLabel: From 'oldest continuing cultures' onward, the Apology's repeated 'future' phrases relegate ghosts and trauma to the past

n0037.navLabel: A future based on mutual respect, resolve and responsibility where all Australians are equal partners

n0038.navLabel: Critics see the Apology as festival of self-forgiveness or empty symbolism, doubting the past can be overwritten

n0039.title: Derrida's Spectral Future
n0039.gist: Derrida's model of an unpredictable, spectral future suggests hope requires accepting haunting rather than erasing the past through linear narratives of moving on.

n0040.navLabel: Unremitting woundedness traps ghosts in melancholy rather than allowing them to haunt the future

n0041.navLabel: Derrida's l'avenir names a real future as the totally unpredictable arrival of the Other

n0042.navLabel: Derrida's relationship to past, present and future is anti-linear, full of irrecoverable traces

n0043.navLabel: The rhetoric of memory recalls and recounts, forgetting anteriority even as it refers to the past

n0044.navLabel: Limitless memory would be infinite self-presence, not memory, so we remember, forget and go on

n0045.title: Indigenous Poetry
n0045.gist: Tony Birch's poem on Beruk shows how Indigenous poetry keeps ancestral ghosts alive in the present, modelling a hauntedness that empowers rather than merely wounds.

n0046.title: Beruk's Ghost
n0046.gist: Birch's poem sequence gives voice to the Indigenous leader Beruk across two centuries, culminating in his spectral return to the Wurundjeri riverbed.

n0048.navLabel: Tony Birch's 'The true history of Beruk' invokes the ghost of Wurundjeri leader Barak from 1835 to 2007

n0049.navLabel: Beruk's 1835 words recall Cook, Buckley and Batman, and warn that whitefellow will shoot us down

n0050.navLabel: Beruk's 2005 spirit moves through the city's stone canyons, slipping into the poisoned riverbed

n0051.navLabel: Beruk greets his son and father in the riverbed, singing 'we will be gone... we will come and be'

n0053.title: Haunting as Active Memory
n0053.gist: Birch's reflections and the poem's closing lines show memory functioning as an active, hopeful haunting rather than static nostalgia.

n0054.navLabel: The poem's gritty persistence and the poet's will to sing counter any reading of mere nostalgia

n0055.navLabel: Birch links the Yarra dredging's exposed pre-European riverbed to his desire for Barak's story to resonate today

n0056.navLabel: Memory works through haunting and melancholy that honours 'that love we do not want to relinquish' without impoverishing the ego
